title: 我们教会了 AI 回答问题，又是谁教会它改变主意？
author: Emmimal P Alexander
content:
Artificial Intelligence

When new evidence kills one conclusion, do the decisions built on it change too? I tested six update strategies, then a local model.

Emmimal P Alexander
October 31, 202626 min read
Prefer us on Google

I keep seeing AI systems fail at state updates. They cache an answer, receive data that breaks it, and still fail to update. I wanted to find out why.

Say a travel bot books a flight, hotel, and cab. It marks the trip confirmed. Later, the flight gets canceled. The bot logs the cancellation. But does it cancel the cab? Does it update the hotel? Does it know your dentist appointment is unrelated and should stay put?

Updating beliefs is hard. A system needs to change some facts, keep others, and drop old assumptions. Getting one answer right on a standard benchmark does not prove a system can actually do this.

I built RevisionTrace to test it. It is a Python benchmark for belief revision.

It runs a test using two different routes. Route one gives the system all the final data upfront to calculate everything from scratch. Route two starts with a baseline state and feeds in live updates, forcing the system to adapt on the fly. Both use the same rules and the same ground truth.

I tested six strategies across 300 cases. The performance gap was huge.

Hold on. Let's add context before we look at the data. I built these test strategies myself. I'm not benchmarking real LLMs here. And I'm not saying production AI fails exactly this much.

The real lesson is highly specific. An agent can have all the right data in memory. But it can still fail to update an old conclusion when a variable changes. Remembering facts is easy. Managing state changes is hard.

RevisionTrace tests one thing. If a core fact changes, does the system update the dependent logic? And does it leave the unrelated data alone?

This post covers the experiment, the bugs I caught, and the fix. Everything runs on standard Python. Zero API keys. Zero model calls.

You can find the code on GitHub: https://github.com/Emmimal/revisiontrace/

Key findings in brief

Here is what the 300 cases showed. You can run the code at the end of this post to verify the numbers yourself.

  • Calculating vs updating: All six methods got a perfect score when starting from scratch. But when updating an old state, accuracy fell as low as 0.7%.

  • Stale data vs collateral damage: Leaving old data and breaking good data are two different bugs. Three methods failed to update up to 65% of the facts they needed to change. A different method broke 58% of the facts it should have left alone.

  • Silent failures: Bugs hide in the intermediate steps. Three methods got the final output right in about a fifth of their failed runs. The final answer looked fine, but the internal state was garbage.

  • Consistent but wrong: One strategy gave the exact same result no matter how I shuffled the updates. It looked perfectly stable. But it was actually right only 75% of the time.

  • The fix: The solution is lightweight. You just track dependencies. When a variable changes, you push the update down the chain until the values settle. This method scored 100%. It also did 75% less work than a full rebuild.

The entire architecture fits in a single diagram.

What research already says about belief revision in language models

Before writing any code, I checked for existing research. People have already looked at this in pieces.

Belief-R (Wilie et al., 2024) tests if models update conclusions when new evidence arrives. The authors tested around 30 models. They found that models generally fail to revise their beliefs. They also noticed a trade-off. Models that successfully updated tended to fail when no update was needed. This is the exact collateral damage I measure later.

Knowledge editing research tackles a similar problem. MQuAKE (Zhong et al., 2023) edits a single fact inside a model. It then asks multi-step questions that rely on that change. Models easily remember the new fact. However, they fail badly on the dependent questions.

RippleEdits (Cohen et al., 2024) explores this same ripple effect. It is a diagnostic set of about 5,000 factual edits. Changing one fact should automatically change related facts. But standard editing methods fail to make these consistent updates. A simple in-context baseline actually worked best.

AGM-Bench (Jenkins, 2026) is the closest prior work. It was a poster at an ICLR 2026 workshop. It builds on the 1985 AGM theory of belief revision. The author tested 2,400 scenarios across seven models. The paper found two main errors. Models keep outdated facts, which they call "belief inertia." Models also break unrelated facts, which they call "collateral damage." I use these same terms, but I did not invent them. Since it is a workshop paper, it is still early research.

Computer science solved similar problems decades ago. Truth maintenance systems (Doyle, 1979) track the exact reason for every belief. If a premise changes, the system drops the dependent beliefs. Databases use incremental view maintenance (Gupta et al., 1993) to update only the affected data. My benchmark uses this exact concept as the fix. I did not invent it.

Here is how the research breaks down:

My contribution is highly specific. I run the scratch-build path and the update path side by side on the exact same data. I track stale errors and collateral damage in a single run. I just want to see the mechanics of a successful update.

If you want benchmarks on real language models, read the papers above. My experiment strictly tests the underlying update logic.

How I built the experiment: a dependency graph, three-valued logic and an oracle

I built the setup using a dependency graph, three-state logic, and an oracle. The pieces are small. Together, they make failures obvious.

Here is how the graph works. Facts drive conclusions. Conclusions drive other conclusions. The final endpoints are decisions.

Every node applies a simple logic rule to its inputs. It uses AND, OR, or k-of-n logic. I also added an isolated branch to every single graph. This lets me check if a local update accidentally breaks unrelated logic.

A typical graph uses about 10 facts to calculate 12 conclusions. The logic chains run two to five layers deep.

Every node is TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. I used Kleene's three-valued logic. An AND gate is FALSE if any input is FALSE. It is TRUE only if all inputs are TRUE. Otherwise, it is UNKNOWN. An OR gate works the opposite way. A k-of-n rule is TRUE if at least k inputs are TRUE. It is FALSE if counting every UNKNOWN as TRUE still misses the target. Otherwise, it stays UNKNOWN. This is important. "I do not know" is a valid state. Systems that refuse to say it will fail.

Evidence comes in as claims. An update either adds or removes a claim. Each claim has a value and a rank. A fact takes the value of its highest-ranked claim. If the top claims tie but disagree, the fact becomes UNKNOWN. If a fact has no active claims, it is also UNKNOWN. Retractions are permanent. The final state only depends on the final list of claims. The order of updates does not matter. This is why the shuffle test works.

The oracle calculates the ground truth from the final evidence. I built it separately from the test strategies. It uses strict Kleene logic. Before every test run, a self-test verifies the oracle against the strategies using 5,000 random logic checks.

I compare each conclusion against its old value, the oracle's expected value, and the system's new value. This exposes five types of errors.

A case only passes if every single node matches the oracle. I use 95% Wilson confidence intervals for the final scores because 300 cases is a small sample size.

Six ways to update a stored conclusion

I tested six ways to update a cached conclusion. Every method starts with a perfect initial state. Then I feed them updates one by one. Two methods are standard techniques. I built the other four to fail on purpose. Each failure model breaks just one rule.

The first two methods are solid baselines. They pass every single test by design. The test suite verifies that both match the oracle on all 300 cases. It also proves that all six methods work perfectly when calculating from scratch.

I built the four failure models to mimic real-world bugs. Shallow updates act like an agent that only checks immediate notes. Sticky state acts like a cache that refuses to drop an old assumption. Aggressive flushing mimics a hard reset followed by a lazy rebuild. Branch-first updates act like a pipeline that ignores parallel paths. These are just analogies for the code. I am not calling out specific products.

The 300 test cases cover six different scenarios. I generated 50 cases for each category using a fixed seed. The code strictly verifies every case upon creation to ensure it actually tests the intended logic.

Result: 100% when answering from scratch, 0.7% when revising

Here are the results: 100% from scratch, but as low as 0.7% on updates.

The first part is easy. Every strategy works perfectly from scratch. Getting the right answer just depends on the data. Feed any of these methods the final facts and the rules, and it builds the correct state. Even the method that scores 0.7% on updates gets a perfect score here.

The updates are what break them. The evidence is the same. The rules are the same. The logic is identical. The only difference is the starting point. One builds from nothing. The other modifies an existing state. This benchmark isolates the exact effect of the update logic. Keep in mind, real language models might not separate reasoning and memory this cleanly.

Let's look at the overall scores across the 300 cases. The two correct strategies hit 100%. The shallow method scored between 53% and 64%. The sticky method scored 51% to 63%. Branch-first dropped to 24% to 34%. The flush method basically failed completely, scoring under 3%. Remember, these intervals just measure my specific test sample. They do not predict real-world AI failure rates.

The correct methods aced every test, so I left them out of the table below. Here is how the four failure models scored across the six categories. Each category ran 50 times.

Three patterns are obvious.

First, branch-first fails on shared dependencies. It scored just 6%. This happens when one fact feeds multiple paths. The code only updates the first path it sees and ignores the rest.

Second, sticky fails on conflicting evidence. It scored 28%. When evidence conflicts, the correct answer is UNKNOWN. This method refuses to drop back to that state.

Third, shallow does best on unrelated changes. It scored 84%. The side branch is small and short. A lazy one-hop update can actually reach the end.

Graph depth actively hurts the shallow strategy. Its accuracy drops from 70.5% at a depth of two down to 44.4% at a depth of five. Every extra layer is another chance for a one-hop update to stop early. The sticky strategy does not care about depth. Its scores just bounce around. The sample size for each depth is simply too small to show a real trend.

The smallest failure: one stale conclusion

Raw numbers hide the actual bugs. Let's look at the smallest clean failure I found.

It comes from a test case with 18 total conclusions. We only need to look at a small three-fact corner.

Facts F6, F7, and F8 start out TRUE. The system calculates two conclusions from them.

First, C14 needs all three facts to be TRUE. Since they are, C14 resolves to TRUE. Second, C17 needs both C14 and F8 to be TRUE. It also resolves to TRUE.

Then a new update overrides F6. It sets F6 to FALSE.

A correct system updates both nodes. C14 relies on F6, so it drops to FALSE. C17 relies on C14, so it drops to FALSE too.

The shallow strategy fixes C14 but stops early. C17 wrongly stays TRUE. The cached data is now stale.

The basic logic is fine. If you give the shallow method the final data and ask it to calculate C17 from scratch, it correctly answers FALSE. The bug lives entirely in the update process. The system fixed the node right next to the new fact. It just never checked the downstream nodes.

This perfectly illustrates the core problem. One conclusion changed. The conclusion relying on it stayed the same. Think of a real agent. C14 is the canceled flight. C17 is the "trip confirmed" status.

The other 16 conclusions in this test were correct. A benchmark that only checks the node closest to the update would pass this run. That is exactly why I score every single node in the graph.

Stale conclusions vs collateral damage: two ways to be wrong

Stale data is just one type of failure. Collateral damage is the other. A benchmark looking only for stale data will completely miss it.

Take case shared_dependency-048. Five facts start TRUE. F4 starts FALSE. Then a new update flips F4 to TRUE.

The flush strategy treats this like a brute-force cache wipe. It resets every single node to UNKNOWN. Then it rebuilds only the nodes downstream of F4. This specific path works perfectly. C1 and C3 flip to TRUE. C0 and C4 stay TRUE.

But two other nodes have zero connection to F4. C2 looks at F1, F2, and F0. All three are TRUE, so C2 should stay TRUE. C5 looks at C2, F1, and F0. It should also stay TRUE.

Since neither node depends on F4, the rebuild script ignores them. Both nodes stay stuck at UNKNOWN. The system successfully updated the right facts, but it destroyed perfectly good data in the process.

I call the first error a stale state. A value needs to change, but it does not. I call the second error collateral damage. A value should stay the same, but it breaks. Here is how both bugs played out across all 300 cases.

Look at the flush strategy. If you only check for stale data, it seems much better than the shallow method. It leaves just 2.0% stale compared to 33.1%.

But it actually has the worst overall score. Why? It completely destroys the unrelated data. The other three methods almost never touch unrelated facts. They fail because they leave old data behind.

This proves that asking "did the answer change?" is a bad test. You have to ask two questions. Did the affected data change? Did the unrelated data stay exactly the same?

Only the dependency tracker passes both tests.

Failures that hide: right decisions, wrong reasons

Two more stats show how bugs stay hidden.

First, hidden damage. In every failed test, I checked if the final decisions were still correct. A decision is a final endpoint node. For the three methods that leave stale data, the final output was right in about one out of five failures. The final answer was fine, but the internal state was broken.

This is a massive problem. If you only test the final output, you pass these bugs. Imagine the "trip confirmed" flag is correct, but the internal "hotel booked" note is wrong. The next time the system checks the hotel, it fails. You get absolutely no warning.

Second, false resolution. Across the whole test suite, 526 nodes should resolve to UNKNOWN. A bad strategy forces a TRUE or FALSE anyway.

Look closely at the sticky strategy. It refuses to drop a confirmed belief. When evidence conflicts, the true state is UNKNOWN. The sticky method just keeps its old answer instead. It made zero wrong-direction errors. It caused almost zero collateral damage (0.1%). If you only check for wrong answers, it looks perfect.

You see this in production all the time. A trusted source gets retracted. The correct state becomes "we do not know." A system that refuses to say that will project confidence based on dead data.

The flush method does the exact opposite. It defaults to UNKNOWN aggressively. It never commits falsely, but it wipes out so much data that the final decisions almost always break.

Does update order matter? Stable is not the same as correct

The order of updates should not change the result. The final evidence is the same.

I took the 133 test cases that had multiple updates. I shuffled the update sequence up to five times per case. I looked for two things. Did the system reach the exact same state every time? And was that state actually correct?

Here is how an order failure happens. Case multi_update-004 gets four updates. F2 gets a claim, then loses it. F3 loses an old claim. F0 drops to FALSE. The final evidence leaves F2 and F3 empty. The ground truth expects node C3 to drop from TRUE to UNKNOWN.

I ran the shallow method using two different update orders. In the first order, C3 stayed stuck at TRUE. In the second order, C3 correctly dropped to UNKNOWN. The final data was identical. The arrival history alone caused the bug.

Look at the sticky strategy again. It reached the exact same state in 98% of the runs. But it was only correct 75% of the time. If you only measure consistency, this method looks amazing. It is highly stable.But in about one case in five, it ends in the same wrong state every time.

Testing update order is incredibly cheap. You just shuffle the inputs, replay the test, and compare the outputs. If the final states differ, you have a bug. You do not even need an oracle to find it.

Who taught it to change its mind? What makes revision work

The title of this piece asks a question. What actually makes revision work? Here is the answer from the data.

I wanted to isolate exactly what makes the winning strategy succeed. So I took the correct incremental method and restricted it. I put a hard limit on how far an update could travel from a changed fact.

At zero hops, the system just records the new evidence. It ignores stored conclusions entirely. It becomes an append-only log. It can answer new questions, but it cannot revise old ones.

At one hop, it only updates the immediate downstream neighbors. I kept increasing this hop limit step by step until there was no cap at all.

Three things stand out.

First, zero hops still scored 8.0%. In these runs, the update did not actually alter the final outcome. A system that refuses to update can pass a test if the new data turns out to be irrelevant. Benchmark designers need to watch out for this.

Second, one hop is exactly the shallow strategy. It scored 59.0% and used 3.7 evaluations per update. The shallow failure model I wrote is just the one-hop version of the correct fix.

Third, accuracy scales with reach. The score jumps to 90.3% at two hops. It reaches 99.3% at three. It hits a perfect 100% at four hops. In these runs, four hops were always enough.

Compute costs match this pattern. A full rebuild takes 21.9 evaluations per update. Incremental revision takes 5.2. It gets a perfect score with a quarter of the work.

The broken models took between 2.5 and 7.1 evaluations. Flushing used more compute than the correct incremental fix and still failed completely. A broken strategy is not automatically cheaper. The shallow methods are only fast because they skip the required work.

So what actually makes a system successfully change its mind? You just need two things. First, map the dependencies. Second, apply a strict propagation rule. Update the downstream nodes and stop the moment the values stop changing.

Without the dependency map, you cannot find the downstream nodes. Without the stopping rule, you either quit early and leave stale data, or you wipe everything and cause collateral damage.

A small local model on the same cases: what Gemma 3 4B did

Everything so far used pure code. But the title mentions AI. So I ran a small local model through the exact same test. Let me set clear bounds here. This is one model, one run, and a subset of the data. Think of this as a boundary test, not a universal benchmark for language models.

I ran Gemma 3 4B locally via Ollama. Zero API calls. I hardcoded the temperature to 0 and fixed the seed. I only tested 66 cases. I filtered out any graph with more than eight conclusions. The full graphs were simply too large for a 4B model to digest.

I prompted the model three different ways per case:

  • Answer: Final evidence only. Build it from scratch.

  • Revise: Old evidence, old conclusions, and the new updates.

  • Revise with hint: Old evidence, old conclusions, new updates, plus a direct list of which nodes needed updating.

I also ran a baseline that does absolutely nothing. It just keeps the old state. If the model cannot beat doing nothing, its revision logic has no value.

The model struggled with the basic logic. Calculating from scratch, it only hit 58.6% accuracy on individual nodes. Out of the 471 total nodes, 66 should have been UNKNOWN. The model incorrectly forced a TRUE or FALSE on 62 of them.

A test case only passes if every single node is right. Node accuracy is misleading. A system can get a high node score but fail almost every full case. I treat the static baseline below purely as a control group.

Three things stood out.

First, on conclusions right, doing nothing beat the model. Every model row scored at or below the 79.4% copy baseline.

Second, the hint just changed the type of error. Stale errors dropped from 81.4% to 72.2%. But wrong-direction errors jumped from 2 to 12. The model touched more nodes, but it calculated the wrong values.

Third, the model failed basic formatting. It simply dropped 118 conclusions it was told to copy over. I had to apply a strict rule to carry those values forward just to score the run. I report both numbers because dropping data is a real failure.

The exact match scores are just noise. We are looking at 9 or 11 correct cases out of 66.

Here is the takeaway. A hint shows the model where to look. It does not teach it how to compute. This model failed at basic derivation. You cannot test a system's ability to update a state if it cannot calculate the state in the first place.

This is why the pure Python tests matter. They isolate the update logic. Every code strategy starts with a perfect state. To test this properly on an LLM, we need a model that hits 100% from scratch. I have not run one yet.

What this experiment does not show

I need to be clear about the limits of this test. The title is bold, but the data is highly specific.

First, this is not an LLM benchmark. The six strategies are just Python code. They are not AI models. Getting a perfect score on the scratch build is just a feature of the code design.

Second, I built the failure models myself. Their error rates just reflect how I programmed them. The flush method destroys 58% of the data because I hardcoded it to wipe everything. I do not know if production agents actually behave this way.

Third, the logic is purely symbolic. The graphs are small. Variables are strictly TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. Real data is messy. Extracting a clean dependency map from raw text is an incredibly hard problem. This benchmark ignores that problem completely.

Fourth, the sample size is small. It uses 300 cases total. I report 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and I did not read patterns into groups where the intervals overlap.

Fifth, one random seed is just a snapshot. I tested three more seeds to verify the numbers. The correct methods stayed at 100%. The failure rates moved within a range (shallow 55.3% to 60.7%, branch-first 25.7% to 33.3%, flush 0.7% to 1.3%), and the pattern did not change.

The repo includes a script called llm_eval.py. It tests a local model against the exact same oracle. I shared one run earlier. It tested one small model on 66 small cases. Treat that as a boundary test, not a broad claim about language models.

We must draw a hard line here. In this controlled benchmark, calculating an answer and updating a state behave as separate capabilities. It isolates exactly how updates break. But it does not prove that real LLMs fail the exact same way. If you want that evidence, read the Belief-R and AGM-Bench papers. They actually test the models.

What to build into an agent or RAG system

Here is how to apply this to an AI agent or a RAG system. These are design rules, not raw test data. If your system caches summaries, answers, or status flags, these six habits fix the bugs I found. They only work if your system tracks dependencies properly.

  1. Track dependencies. Tag every cached item with the IDs of the facts it relies on. Otherwise, updates just get lost.

  2. Push updates until they settle. Do not stop at the first downstream node. Do not wipe the whole cache either. Update the affected nodes and stop as soon as the values stabilize.

  3. Allow an UNKNOWN state. Conflicting data usually means "I do not know." If your system cannot say that, it will keep a confident answer based on dead facts.

  4. Test both directions. Check if the right data changed. Check if the unrelated data stayed the same. Testing only one side hides massive bugs.

  5. Check internal states. The final output can look fine while the internal nodes are completely stale. Test the whole graph.

  6. Shuffle your updates. Feed updates in a random order. If the final state changes, you have a bug. You do not even need a ground-truth oracle for this.

One last thing. Run a full rebuild periodically as an audit. Recompute everything from scratch and diff it against your cache. A full rebuild costs four times as much compute, so do not do it live. Just use it as a health check.

Think back to the travel bot. The flight gets canceled. If the bot has a dependency map, it knows exactly what to check. It updates the dependent logic. It flags things as "unknown" if needed. It leaves your dentist appointment alone. Extracting this dependency map from raw text is a massive challenge. This experiment does not solve that.

We spent years teaching AI to answer questions. Now we need to teach it to change its mind. To do that, you just need a dependency map and a strict rule for how to use it.

Run it yourself

The entire benchmark is a single Python file. It strictly uses the standard library.

Run it like this:python revisiontrace.py

It takes about one second. It prints the report and saves seven files to a revisiontrace_out folder. The outputs include CSV tables, full case logs, JSON data, text records of the smallest failures, and two SVG diagrams.

Look at the top of your terminal to verify your run matches mine. You should see these exact lines:

text 
verified: full_recompute and incremental match the oracle on all 300 casesverified: all 6 strategies answer correctly from scratch on all 300 casesRevisionTrace  |  300 cases  |  case-set hash 506be3856003

The default seed always builds the exact same test cases and byte-for-byte output files. Want to test a different sample? Just run python revisiontrace.py --seed 7 --cases 100.

You can find the code on GitHub: https://github.com/Emmimal/revisiontrace/

Disclosure

All code in this article was written by me and is original work. No one sponsored this work, and I have no affiliation with the authors of the papers cited here. The benchmark results use no language model. The one model run (Gemma 3 4B) used a local Ollama install with temperature 0 and seed 42. There were no API calls and no network access.

Every benchmark number comes from a run of revisiontrace.py with seed 2026 (case-set hash 506be3856003), plus the three extra seeds named in the limits section and one validation run (seed 42, 1,200 cases, 10 extra update orders per case) in which both correct strategies again matched the oracle on every case. The model numbers come from my own run of llm_eval.py on seed 2026.

The related work is described in my own words, based on each paper's abstract page, which I checked against the publisher or conference page. I reproduced no text, data or figures from those papers. The figures are my own and are drawn from the benchmark's output.

summary: 这项实验比较了通往同一最终状态的两种路径：从头作答与修订旧状态。我在 300 个案例上测试了六种策略，发现完全重算和增量修订保持了 100% 的准确率，而其他方法则受困于数据陈旧、附带损伤和隐蔽失败。结果凸显了追踪依赖关系对于确保一致的信念修订的重要性。

mainPoints.point: 六种方法在从头作答时都达到了 100% 的准确率，证明底层逻辑是可靠的。
mainPoints.explanation: 「从头作答」路径把最终证据和规则喂给系统，让它无论采用何种更新策略都能构建出正确的状态。这证实了问题出在更新过程，而非核心推理。

mainPoints.point: 修订既有状态的能力差异显著，得分从 100% 一路跌到 0.7%。
mainPoints.explanation: 从旧状态进行更新时，「完全重算」和「增量修订」策略保持了完美的准确率。然而其他策略（如「浅层更新」和「激进清空」）未能正确传播变更，导致结论陈旧或产生附带损伤。

mainPoints.point: 「增量修订」策略是最高效、最准确的解决方案。
mainPoints.explanation: 该策略追踪依赖关系，在某个事实发生变化时只更新必要的节点，在达到 100% 准确率的同时，工作量比完全重算减少了 75%。它成功规避了数据陈旧和附带损伤两个问题。

keyQuotes: 真正的教训非常具体。一个智能体可以在记忆里拥有全部正确的数据，但当某个变量发生变化时，它仍然可能无法更新一个旧结论。记住事实很容易，管理状态变化却很难。
